newsitem.title: JAPAN: Moody's sees default risk in some samurai bonds.
newsitem.headline: Moody's sees default risk in some samurai bonds.

text.p: Moody's Investors Service said on Thursday there was the risk of a default in some yen-denominated samurai bonds placed publicly.
"I think it may not be too long before we see one of those public instruments default," Kenneth Pinkes, chief credit officer at Moody's, told reporters in Tokyo.

The samurai bond market, mainly targeting retail investors here, has boomed because of low domestic interest rates, and underwriting sources said the volume of issues this year up to the end of October was a record 3.16 trillion yen.
That compares with the 1.61 trillion yen worth of issues for all of 1995.
Pinkes said Moody's was looking for ways to alert investors who invest in speculative-grade samurai issues to the risks that they may not fully appreciate.

Concerns about repayment problems have been increasing, particularly after Bulgaria's Mineralbank failed to redeem five billion yen worth of samurai bonds to Japanese creditors when they matured in June.
Japan's Finance Ministry avoided direct comment on the problem because the bonds were privately placed.
